claims.text: High compositional complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys produces heterogeneous lattice strain.
Heterogeneous lattice strain promotes unusual dislocation structures, including multiple kinks, jogs, and bidirectional cross-slip.
The unusual dislocation behavior provides a strengthening mechanism.
The stabilized dislocation behavior improves high-temperature strength retention relative to conventional refractory alloys.
The stabilized dislocation behavior improves thermoelastic performance at high temperature.
As-synthesized NbTaTiVZr or similar RHEAs possess pronounced inherent lattice strain.
A high-complexity RHEA should be compared with a conventional refractory alloy or modified HEA having reduced compositional disorder and minimal lattice strain.
Using identical processing and heat treatment isolates lattice distortion as the governing variable in the proposed comparison.
The proposed mechanism applies during tensile or compressive loading at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
Localized lattice distortions generate internal stress fields that modify dislocation core structures.
Modification of dislocation core structures reduces dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility increases alloy strength.
Greater lattice distortion limits expansion of the plastic zone during deformation.
Limiting plastic-zone expansion modifies the alloy's thermoelastic response.
The high-distortion RHEA should retain more strength at elevated temperature than the baseline alloy.
The high-distortion RHEA should show more multiple kinks, jogs, and cross-slip events in in-situ TEM than the baseline alloy.
The high-distortion RHEA should exhibit modified elastic moduli and thermal-expansion behavior relative to the baseline.

Failure to detect statistically significant differences in dislocation structures, strength retention, or thermoelastic behavior would falsify the proposed governing role of heterogeneous lattice strain.
